Caitlin Carr-Smith is a Movie Features Writer at Collider who loves to discuss film through detailed analysis and fresh perspectives. Prior to Collider, she honed her skills in pop culture writing at the satirical newspaper The Flipside at Northwestern University, where she also earned a degree in Film & Television.

With the highly anticipated upcoming release of Sunrise on the Reaping, it's clear that audiences still clamor for more stories from the world of The Hunger Games. Since the release of the first book in 2008, it’s become one of the most beloved and successful franchises in 21st century pop culture, with five books, six movies, and thousands of fans. On top of the extensive world building and rich characters, readers and moviegoers alike are drawn to the series’ intelligent and compelling writing, which has given fans iconic lines such as “may the odds be ever in your favor” and “I volunteer as tribute.” But it’s a quote from the second film that remains the most poignant.

At the end of the first installment in the original Hunger Games trilogy, Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence) and her fellow District 12 tribute Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson) have survived the 74th Hunger Games to become the first dual winners. In the sequel, The Hunger Games: Catching Fire, Katniss and Peeta are forced to return to the arena for the 75th Hunger Games following the stipulation that each District’s tributes will be selected from their existing pools of victors. As in their previous Games, Katniss and Peeta are supported by an elder District 12 victor, Haymitch Abernathy (Woody Harrelson), who delivers a line that is the most important of any Hunger Games dialogue due to its impact on the outcome of Catching Fire and the connections it has to the overall franchise--and possibly even beyond.
The Words That Shape Katniss Everdeen's Fate
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/Catching-Fire-Hunger0Games.jpeg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: Peeta and Katniss doing the Mockingjay symbol while Effie stands between them

blocks.x: Image via Lionsgate

Winning the Games does not guarantee peace or safety. The beginning of Catching Fire sees Katniss struggling with symptoms of PTSD from her time in the arena, including nightmares and hallucinations, as Panem’s leader President Snow (Donald Sutherland) watches her every move. When Katniss and Peeta become tributes in the 75th Games, their mentor Haymitch is at their side once again to support them. He encourages them to make alliances, a different strategy from their previous time in the arena, but Katniss is reluctant to trust anyone other than Peeta. On the night before the Games, Haymitch says his goodbyes to Katniss and Peeta, and gives a piece of advice to Katniss.
“When you’re out in that arena, remember who the real enemy is.”

The impact of this quote isn’t felt immediately, but rather towards the end of the film. Katniss, Peeta, and their allies are setting up a trap for other tributes using a wire wrapped around a tree in the arena that is struck by lightning every night. Katniss is on the verge of shooting her ally Finnick Odair (Sam Claflin), believing he has betrayed her and Peeta, until he repeats what Haymitch told her: “remember who the real enemy is.” Katniss then turns her bow from Finnick to the sky, attaches the wire connected to the tree to one of her arrows, and shoots the forcefield surrounding the arena just as the tree is struck by lightning. The forcefield is overpowered by electricity and collapses, the broadcast is cut off, and the 75th Hunger Games are officially over.

https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/the-hunger-games-haymitch-coaches-katniss-before-the-games.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: Haymitch (Woody Harrelson) and Katniss (Jennifer Lawrence) before the Games.

blocks.x: Image credit via Lionsgate.

Haymitch’s words have a twofold effect. On a very basic level, they save Katniss’s life by stopping her from turning on a true ally. Finnick’s repetition of Haymitch’s exact words proves to Katniss that he is trustworthy, since he has clearly spoken with Haymitch before the Games. If she had killed Finnick, her alliances with other tributes would have been ruined, likely with fatal consequences. But beyond that, the words make Katniss reconsider where her bow should really be pointed. Yes, in the arena, the tributes are trying to kill each other, but they shouldn’t even be in the arena in the first place. Every tribute is forced into the Hunger Games by a government that gets pleasure from watching twenty-three children die and the "winner" suffering permanent trauma. Ultimately, the tributes don't want to kill each other, but the system they live in pits them against each other so that they have to do unspeakable things to survive, even though they really should be banding together to attack their oppressors. When Katniss hears Haymitch's words from Finnick, she is reminded of who the real enemy is—the Capitol—and is inspired to shoot at the arena forcefield instead of a Tribute, ending the Games on her own terms.

When Katniss fires her arrow into the sky, she alters her destiny and the fate of the entire country. After the arena is destroyed, a rebel contingent rescues Katniss and brings her to safety. Inspired by Katniss' actions, anti-Captiol riots and protests increase in the districts, and the Capitol bombs District 12, killing the majority of the population. This leads to Katniss actively joining and leading the rebellion in the two-part finale, The Hunger Games: Mockingjay—Part One (2014) and Mockingjay—Part 2 (2015), which leads to the series ending in the defeat of the Capitol and the establishment of a new government. Without Haymitch's words, Katniss would have shot at Finnick instead of the forcefield, the events following the arena's destruction would not have come to pass, and the entire Hunger Games franchise could have ended very differently.
Haymitch's 'Catching Fire' Line Captures A Core Theme of the Franchise
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/5652a9bd97e0d-image.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: Jennifer Lawrence as Katniss Everdeen in Mockingjay: Part 2 (2015).

blocks.x: Image credit via Lionsgate.

Enemies and allies are concepts explored throughout the Hunger Games franchise both inside and outside the arena, as knowing one's true enemy is protection and salvation. When Katniss and Peeta are the two remaining tributes left in the 74th Hunger Games and told only one can remain, they decide to remain allies and to strike back at the Capitol, their true enemy, by taking their lives with poisonous berries. This ends up saving their lives, as the Gamemakers declare them both winners to avoid the embarrassment of having no winner at all. In Mockingjay—Part 2, after the defeat of the Capitol, Katniss learns that the rebel leader and new interim President, Alma Coin (Julianne Moore), refuses to hold a democratic election and that she purposely orchestrated a bombing during the war that killed civilian children to assure her own political power. When Coin asks Katniss to publicly execute President Snow, Katniss agrees, but shoots Coin instead, and Snow is trampled to death in the chaos that follows. With Snow captured and powerless, Katniss saw that Coin was the real enemy in the post-war world, as she would be no better than any other Capitol leader that came before, and so Katniss turned her bow on her to prevent Panem from being subjected to another cruel dictator.

Throughout the franchise, before and after she heard Haymitch's words, Katniss comes to learn the importance of identifying the true enemy, and time and time again, the true enemy is a larger system of corruption and oppression that often tries to use an individual as a decoy. Katniss repeatedly saves her own life and the lives of others by recognizing it is not the tributes but the Games, not one person but a system, that is the real threat. Intriguing, well-developed themes like these can account for why The Hunger Games has stayed in the public consciousness and earned lifelong fans while other young adult dystopian stories have faded into obscurity. Readers and viewers are given complex ideas to think about long after they've finished the series that can be applied to their own lives, even though their world may not look exactly like Panem, and Haymitch's advice to Katniss may just be the most relevant and important. In our increasingly divided contemporary culture, this quote can give those who hear it a much-needed moment to stop and think about who or what they are being told is their enemy, and who or what may benefit from their attention turned elsewhere.
